alalal-c46539-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 14: whether spirit, both created and uncreated, can be said to be in place, and whether two spirits can be in the same place.

alalal-c46539-d1e117.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's (Augustine's) statement that only the most foolish would say the Holy Spirit has no place.

alalal-c46539-d1e129.summary: First argument: the text implies that only body resists body in place, so two created spirits could be in the same place; and if two, then infinitely many or all, which everyone denies.

alalal-c46539-d1e154.summary: Second argument: if two created spirits cannot share a place, it is either because they are spirits, but God and the soul share a place, or because they are created, but soul and body share a place; so two spirits can.

alalal-c46539-d1e180.summary: Third argument: spirit and body are more composite together than two spirits, so if spirit and body can share a place, all the more two spirits. The reply that created spirits would be confused is unreasonable, since the created differs more from the uncreated than from another created being.

alalal-c46539-d1e219.summary: Introduces a second set of objections: it seems meaningless to say a spirit is in place.

alalal-c46539-d1e226.summary: First objection: the Philosopher says a point and its place do not differ; an angel is more indivisible than a point, lacking even position in the continuum, so no angel is in place.

alalal-c46539-d1e246.summary: Second objection: place is a quantity bounding the located from outside, so the contained must have a boundary of the same ratio and quantity; only a quantified body has this, so an angel is not in place.

alalal-c46539-d1e270.summary: Third objection: place is understood mathematically, with common boundaries joining parts of place and located (Boethius), or physically, as what conserves and attracts the located by nature, as light things rise and heavy things fall. In neither sense can spirits be in place.

alalal-c46539-d1e319.summary: Fourth objection: whatever determines a place for itself determines it as equal to itself, which requires the same ratio of quantity; an angel does not relate to bodily place in that way.

alalal-c46539-d1e335.summary: Fifth objection: how large is an angel's place? If of some size, it could not be in a smaller one, which is false. Being in place accidentally by an assumed body is not at issue. If it is in place definitively by its work, then God would also be defined in place, since his work is here and not elsewhere, which is false.

alalal-c46539-d1e368.summary: Solution: things are in place in many ways. First, generable and corruptible things need a place that preserves and contains them, chiefly because their extremities are determined by acting and suffering contraries and would dissipate without an external container.
claims: Generable and corruptible bodies need a preserving place because their contrary qualities would otherwise dissipate at their boundaries.

alalal-c46539-d1e397.summary: Explains how place preserves when its boundary also has contraries: the containing vessel-place derives this from place simply, which is twofold, absolute up at the lunar sphere and absolute down at the centre, which preserves through being equally regarded by the whole heaven. Also, things are weaker at their extremes, so nature gives them a container. In this sense motion is to and from place, only generables are in place, only rectilinear movers move to it, and the lunar sphere and higher are in no place.
claims: In the natural sense only generable and corruptible bodies are in place, and the heavens are not.

alalal-c46539-d1e454.summary: Second, place as mathematical space, as Boethius seems to mean, contains but does not preserve, merely surrounding from outside; in this sense all bodies except the last sphere are circumscribed by place.

alalal-c46539-d1e474.summary: Third, place as distance of position without inclusion; in this sense the last sphere is and moves in place according to form, not subject (Physics VI), its parts taking different positions while the whole remains. In none of these ways is a created spirit in place.
claims: Created spirits are not in place naturally, mathematically, or positionally.

alalal-c46539-d1e512.summary: Fourth, place accidentally, as our accidents and forms are where we are; angels are not in place this way, or they would always need an assumed body. Rather the angel is in place definitively, by definition of its work: since its operation, both from the agent's and from the effect's side, does not extend beyond the place, the operating substance is understood to be within it, as Damascene says, here and not elsewhere.
claims: An angel is in place definitively, through the limitation of its operation.

alalal-c46539-d1e551.summary: States that this answers all the objections about the angel's place except the last.

alalal-c46539-d1e560.summary: Reply to the last objection: God's work is defined on the side of the effect and what he acts on, but his operating act is not, since it is his substance and everywhere. An angel's work is defined in place on the side of the operating substance, the effect, and its object; place relates to it not by size but as defining, distinguishing it from other places.
claims: God's operating act is his ubiquitous substance, whereas an angel's operation is limited and so defines its place.

alalal-c46539-d1e595.summary: To the first question, Albert agrees with the doctors that two spirits cannot be in the same place, not because nature resists them in bodily place, which they do not fill, but because their operations would be confused.
claims: Two created spirits cannot be in the same place, because their operations would be confused.

alalal-c46539-d1e611.summary: Reply: God's operating act can be neither confused nor distinguished, since it is his essence, mixable with nothing, and is not referred to one place; it relates to every place in one way, though places relate to him differently. Spirits are prevented from sharing a place insofar as they are created spirits, having a limited essence that cannot be referred to operation in every place.
claims: Created spirits cannot share a place because their essence, and so their operation, is limited.

alalal-c46539.summary: Article 14 asks whether created and uncreated spirits can be said to be in place, and whether two spirits can occupy the same place. Objections argue both that nothing should prevent spirits from sharing a place and that spirits, being indivisible and unquantified, cannot be in place at all. Albert distinguishes senses of place. Natural place preserves generable bodies against the dissipation of their contrary qualities, so the heavens are not in it. Mathematical place merely surrounds, and positional place applies to the last sphere, which moves according to form. Place can also be accidental. Created spirits are in place in none of these ways, but definitively: their limited operation does not reach beyond a given place, so they are here and not elsewhere. God's effects are defined in place, but his operating act, being his substance, is everywhere. Two created spirits cannot be in the same place, not because they fill it, but because their limited operations would be confused.
claims: Angels are in place definitively, through the limitation of their operation, not by circumscription.
God's operating act is his substance and is everywhere, so God is not defined by place.
Two created spirits cannot be in the same place because their operations would be confused.
In the natural sense only generable and corruptible bodies are in place.
